content: Chemistry education, often referred to as Chemical Education, encompasses the study and analysis of teaching and learning processes in chemistry across schools, colleges, and universities. It involves understanding how students learn chemistry, identifying effective teaching methods, and improving learning outcomes by modifying instructional approaches and providing appropriate training for chemistry educators. This field includes various teaching modalities such as classroom lectures, demonstrations, and laboratory activities. There is a continuous need to enhance the skills of educators involved in teaching chemistry, and chemistry education addresses this necessity. Philosophical Perspectives in Chemistry Education 1. Practitioner’s Perspective: This viewpoint emphasizes that the individuals responsible for teaching chemistry—teachers, instructors, and professors—define the field of chemistry education through their actions and practices. 2. Self-Identified Chemical Educators: This perspective involves a group of educators and faculty members who focus on contributing to the field through publications, essays, and observations about teaching practices. Unlike traditional researchers in areas like organic or inorganic chemistry, these educators prioritize sharing insights and innovations in teaching. A criticism of this perspective is that many professors lack formal training or background in education, which limits their understanding of effective teaching strategies and student learning processes. 3. Chemical Education Research (CER): This approach applies theories and methods from pre-college science education research to post-secondary settings. CER practitioners study the teaching practices of others rather than focusing solely on their own classrooms. Research in this area often involves human subjects from secondary and post-secondary institutions and employs both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods. Quantitative methods include statistical analysis of collected data, while qualitative methods involve interviews, observations, and journaling. 4. Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL): This emerging perspective encourages mainstream faculty members to develop a deeper understanding of their teaching practices, conduct research on their instructional methods, and reflect on what constitutes meaningful student learning. SoTL aims to bridge the gap between teaching and research by fostering informed and reflective teaching practices. Journals in Chemistry Education Numerous journals publish research and articles related to chemistry education. Historically, many of these journals had limited circulation within their countries of publication. Some journals focus on specific education levels (e.g., schools vs. universities), while others cover all levels. These journals typically include a mix of articles on classroom and laboratory practices as well as educational research. Notable examples include: Journal of Chemical Education (published by the American Chemical Society since 1924) Chemistry Education Research and Practice Education in Chemistry The Chemical Educator Research in chemistry education is also published in broader science education journals. Chemistry Education Around the World Germany: Berlin Graduate School of Natural Sciences and Engineering (BIG-NSE) The BIG-NSE, part of the Unifying Concepts in Catalysis (UniCat) Cluster of Excellence, focuses on catalysis research. Faculty members from six participating institutions supervise and mentor students in various research fields, ranging from natural sciences to engineering. United States: Selected Universities University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA): The Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry develops new curricula and integrates technological tools like distance learning and multimedia. Notable faculty include: Dr. Arlene A. Russell, who researches instructional materials such as the web-based tool Calibrated Peer Review (CPR). Dr. Eric Scerri, who explores the philosophy of chemistry and the teaching of atomic and electronic structure. Dr. Alfred Bacher, who develops new experiments and teaching aids for undergraduate courses. University of California, San Diego (UCSD): The Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry includes chemical education as a primary research area. Faculty members such as Dr. John Czworowski, Dr. Barbara Sawrey, and Dr. Haim Weizman focus on initiatives like problem-based learning, multimedia tools, and improving organic chemistry instruction. Texas A&M University: While the university does not have a dedicated chemical education division, it includes this area as a research interest among faculty. Texas A&M also offers a non-thesis Master’s degree with an emphasis on chemical education, aiming to train students in fundamental chemistry and modern educational theory. University of California, Berkeley: Faculty members such as Dr. Angelica Stacy and Dr. Robert Bergmann lead efforts in developing chemistry curricula and promoting active learning models. Dr. Stacy’s group focuses on high school and college chemistry curricula and student assessment, while Dr. Bergmann supports outreach activities and active learning strategies. University of Pittsburgh: Although the Department of Chemistry does not have faculty dedicated to chemical education research, it raises awareness through a ChemEd seminar featuring nationally recognized researchers. University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC): Faculty members like Dr. Todd Austell, Dr. Brian Hogan, and Dr. Domenic Tiani work on dynamic curricula, active learning, and critical thinking skills. Lecturer Bessie Mbadugha’s specific interests are not detailed. University of Georgia: Dr. Charles H. Atwood focuses on introducing new technologies for educational presentations, assessment, and laboratory instruction. His recent projects include computerized testing and homework systems. University of Iowa: The university emphasizes improving general chemistry courses, graduate student education, and courses for non-science majors. Dr. Norbert J. Pienta conducts research on problem-solving, multimedia use, and training teaching assistants. Degree Programs in Chemistry Education Graduate programs offering MS and/or PhD degrees in chemical education are available in the United States. These programs aim to train students in fundamental chemistry and modern educational practices, often combining research in traditional chemistry subfields with chemical education. A comprehensive list of such programs is maintained by Miami University of Ohio.
